fields.title: Product concept: one page that shows where it can die
fields.keyTakeaway: A concept is needed not to describe a product, but to expose the assumptions it rests on. The most valuable line is the one stating what you don't know and what you test first.
fields.checkQuestion: The concept states "unfair advantage — a strong team." Why is this not an advantage?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **what should the product be?** In block V2, we designed a solution within a known product; here, we build a product as a whole when it doesn't exist yet or is changing.
fields.blocks/1/text: End-to-end example: Surma is a fictional transport company whose internal Dispetcher tool we analyzed in V1 and V2. Now management is discussing whether to turn the internal tool into a product for other carriers.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Nine boxes; fill them in this order
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Problem** and **existing alternatives** — how the job is solved now. An empty alternatives box means you didn't look for them.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Customer segments** and **early adopters** — who hurts the most right now.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Unique value proposition** — one sentence clear to the customer, not just to you.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Solution** — three bullet points, no more. This is the most replaceable part.
fields.blocks/2/items/4: **Channels**, **revenue streams**, **cost structure** — how money flows in and out.
fields.blocks/2/items/5: **Key metrics** and **unfair advantage** — how we'll know it works, and what a competitor cannot quickly copy.
fields.blocks/3/text: **Unfair advantage is the box filled incorrectly most often.** Team, money, and experience are copied through hiring. What cannot be copied: access to data others don't have, a contract that cannot be duplicated, a community accumulated over years, deep integration into someone else's process.
fields.blocks/4/text:
Problem: carriers with 30–80 vehicles plan routes in spreadsheets, empty mileage is 15–20%.
Alternatives: spreadsheets, paper notebook, expensive systems for large fleets.
Early adopters: companies where a dispatcher leaves and training a new one takes long.
Value: "route planning with return load suggestions in five minutes."
Unfair advantage: three years of proprietary data on which return legs actually get loaded on these routes — nobody has this except carriers of similar size.
Main unverified risk: will a carrier want to hand over route data to a company that carries freight itself? This is tested first, because if the answer is "no," everything collapses.
fields.blocks/4/title: Surma: product concept from an internal tool
fields.blocks/5/text: Usually, a team starts with what it knows how to do: writing code. The correct order is the opposite — start with what can kill the idea entirely. For Surma, this is a conflict of interest with future customers, and no amount of development will solve it.
fields.blocks/5/title: Test the most dangerous assumption first, not the most convenient one
fields.blocks/6/text: A canvas is a set of hypotheses on a single page, not a project plan. Its value is measured by how many boxes you replaced with verified facts over a quarter; a beautifully filled and untouched canvas is a bad sign.
